parts.problem_md:
A flowchart of a series of reactions of chromium and some of its compounds is shown.

![q1-paper-6-jan-2022-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/025-q1-paper-6-jan-2022-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

Give the formula of a complex ion of chromium present in solution **A**.
parts.solution_md:
The formula of a complex ion of chromium present in solution **A** is:

Any **one** of the following:

- [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- [CrCl(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>]<sup>+</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- CrCl<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- [CrCl<sub>3</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>–</sup> / [CrCl<sub>3</sub>]<sup>–</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- [CrCl<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> / [CrCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- [CrCl<sub>5</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)]<sup>3–</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The most common answers to this question are [Cr(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* and [CrCl*<sub>*3*</sub>*(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*3*</sub>*]*<sup>*–*</sup>* / [CrCl*<sub>*3*</sub>*]*<sup>*–*</sup>* *
- *The oxidation state of the central chromium causes the main problem with this question as it is actually Cr*<sup>*2+*</sup>* *

  - *This is one of the least common central metal ions that has been used in an exam question*

parts.problem_md: Give the formula of precipitate **B**.
parts.solution_md:
The formula of precipitate **B** is:

- Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>(OH)<sub>3</sub> / Cr(OH)<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Standing blue solution of **A** in air allows the chromium ion to oxidise from Cr*<sup>*2+*</sup>* to Cr*<sup>*3+*</sup>* *
- *Careful: **The reaction **with dilute ammonia solution / NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* (aq)** to form precipitate **B** is a distraction*

  - *Initially, ammonia acts as a base to remove one H*<sup>*+*</sup>* ion per ammonia molecule used*
  - *Remember:** Precipitates do not, usually, have a charge which means that three water ligands have lost a proton  [Cr(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*3+ *</sup>*(aq) + 3NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* (aq) → [Cr(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*3*</sub>*(OH)*<sub>*3*</sub>*] (s) +3NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+ *</sup>*(aq)*

parts.problem_md: Identify reagent **C**, by name or formula.
parts.solution_md:
Reagent **C** is:

- Hydrogen peroxide / H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *A dark green solution is formed by the reaction of precipitate **B** with excess NaOH (aq) is [Cr(OH)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*3–*</sup>* *
- *When warmed with hydrogen peroxide, the dark green solution of [Cr(OH)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*3–*</sup>* oxidises to the yellow solution containing the chromate ion, CrO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>* *

  - *2[Cr(OH)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*3–*</sup>* + 3H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2CrO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>* + 2OH*<sup>*–*</sup>* + 8H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problem_md: Suggest the identity, by name or formula, of precipitate** D**.
parts.solution_md:
Precipitate **D** is:

- Barium chromate(VI) / BaCrO<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Precipitate **D** is formed by the reaction of Ba(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq) with the yellow solution containing the chromate ion, CrO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>* *
- *There is no specific indication of the salt that contains the chromate ion*

  - *Using MCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* for metal chromate: Ba(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq) + MCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* (aq) → M(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + BaCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* *
  - *Metal nitrates are soluble so precipitate **D **cannot be M(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* - plus you don't actually know the metal M Ba(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq) + MCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* (aq) → M(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq) + BaCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* *
  - *This means that the only possible chemical that could be precipitate **D** is BaCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>*  Ba(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq) + MCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* (aq) → M(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq) + BaCrO*<sub>*4*</sub>* (s)*

parts.problem_md: State the colour of solution** E**.
parts.solution_md:
The colour of solution **E** is:

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Chromate / CrO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* and dichromate / Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2- *</sup>*ions can be interconverted by the following equilibrium 2CrO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* (aq) + 2H*<sup>*+ *</sup>*(aq) ⇌ Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (l) *
- *You should know that the dichromate / Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2- *</sup>*ions are orange*

  - *Remember: **Dichromate ions can be used to identify:*
  
    - *Primary and secondary alcohols from tertiary ones*
    - *Aldehydes from ketones*

parts.problem_md: State the colour of solution** F**.
parts.solution_md:
The colour of solution **F** is:

- *Solution **E** contains orange dichromate / Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2- *</sup>*ions *

This question is about copper and some of its compounds.

Two tests were carried out on separate samples of an aqueous solution of copper(II) sulfate.

(i) **Test 1**

A few drops of aqueous sodium hydroxide were added to a sample of the copper(II) sulfate solution.

State what you would see.

**(1)**

(ii)** Test 2**

A few drops of concentrated hydrochloric acid were added to another sample of the copper(II) sulfate solution. More of the concentrated hydrochloric acid was added until it was present in excess.

Describe the changes that would be observed during this test.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) When a few drops of aqueous sodium hydroxide are added to a sample of copper(II) sulfate solution, you would see:

- The formation of a (light / pale) blue precipitate / ppt / solid; **[1 mark]**

ii)** **When a few drops of concentrated hydrochloric acid are added to a sample of copper(II) sulfate solution, the changes that would be observed are:

- The blue solution turns green; **[1 mark]**
- Which turns yellow; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Copper(II) complexes are generally a classic pale blue colour*
- *The exceptions are:*

  - *[CuCl*<sub>*4*</sub>*]*<sup>*2–*</sup>* which is yellow*
  
    - *Careful: **When you are **asked for the changes observed** you can say green because a green colour will be observed as the original blue [Cu(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* complex is turning into the yellow [CuCl*<sub>*4*</sub>*]*<sup>*2–*</sup>* complex*
    - *But, if you are **asked specifically for the colour** of the [CuCl*<sub>*4*</sub>*]*<sup>*2–*</sup>* then any mention of green will cost you the mark*
  - *[Cu(NH*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*4*</sub>*(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*2*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* which is dark blue*

parts.problem_md:
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. A student determined the percentage of copper in a sample of brass.

**Procedure**

- weigh the sample of brass
- place the brass in a beaker and add concentrated nitric acid until all the brass dissolves
- transfer the solution and washings to a 250.0 cm<sup>3 </sup>volumetric flask
- make the solution up to the mark with distilled water and mix well
- pipette 25.0 cm<sup>3 </sup>of the solution into a conical flask
- neutralise the excess nitric acid in the solution
- add 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of potassium iodide solution (an excess) to the conical flask
- titrate the iodine produced with 0.100 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> sodium thiosulfate solution using starch indicator
- repeat the titration until concordant titres are obtained.

i) Copper and zinc both react with concentrated nitric acid to form the metal nitrates, nitrogen dioxide and water. Write the balanced equation for the reaction of zinc with concentrated nitric acid. State symbols are not required.

**(1)**

ii) Name the most suitable piece of apparatus to measure the 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of potassium iodide solution.

**(1)**

iii) State at what point in the titration the starch solution should be added.

**(1)**

iv) Only Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions in the solution react with the aqueous potassium iodide.

2Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 4I<sup>–</sup> → 2CuI + I<sub>2</sub>

The iodine reacts with sodium thiosulfate solution.

2S<sub>2</sub>$O_{3}^{2-}$+ I<sub>2</sub> → S<sub>4</sub>$O_{6}^{2-}$+ 2I<sup>–</sup>

**Results **

Mass of brass sample = 3.90 g

Mean titre of 0.100 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> sodium thiosulfate solution = 28.60 cm<sup>3 </sup>

Calculate the percentage, by mass, of copper in this sample of brass.

Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.

**(5)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction of zinc with concentrated nitric acid is:

- Zn + 4HNO<sub>3</sub> → Zn(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O 
**OR **
Zn + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 2NO<sub>3</sub><sup>− </sup>→ Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The most suitable piece of apparatus to measure the 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of potassium iodide solution is:

- (10 / 25 cm<sup>3</sup>) measuring cylinder; **[1 mark]**

iii) The starch solution should be added when:

- Straw-coloured / pale yellow 
**OR**
Close to / just before / near / approaching the end point; **[1 mark]**

iv) To calculate the percentage, by mass, of copper in this sample of brass:

- Moles of S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> = 0.00286 **OR** 2.86 x 10<sup>−3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of Cu<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.00286 **OR** 2.86 x 10<sup>−3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of Cu<sup>2+</sup> in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.0286 **OR** 2.86 x 10<sup>−2</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of Cu = 1.8161 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Percentage of copper in brass = 45.567% 
**AND**
Answer to 2 / 3 significant figures (45.6% **OR **46%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The question tells you that c**opper and zinc both react with concentrated nitric acid to form the metal nitrates, nitrogen dioxide and water**  Zn + HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → Zn(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *There are three NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* and two hydrogens (in water) on the right-hand side Adding a second NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* brings makes four NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* on the right-hand side Adding a second water molecule makes four hydrogen atoms on the right-hand side Zn + HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → Zn(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Using four HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* now balances the overall equation Zn + 4HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → Zn(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *The potassium iodide solution is in excess so there is no need to measure it accurately*
  - *This means that a measuring cylinder is the most appropriate piece of equipment *
  
    - *Careful:** If you give a size for the measuring cylinder, it cannot be bigger than 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
- *For part (iii)*

  - *The colour of the reaction mixture becomes too pale to accurately determine the end point*
  - *At this point, the starch solution is added to make it easier to see the end point*
- *For part (iv)*

  - *From the titration information, calculate the moles of S*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>* *$\frac{28.6}{1000}\times0.1\,$* = 0.00286 *
  - *The moles of Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* in 25.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = the moles of S*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>* = 0.00286*
  - *The moles of Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* in 250 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* will be ten times greater = 0.00286 x 10 = 0.0286*
  - *Using mass = moles x **A*<sub>*r*</sub>* The moles of Cu = 0.0286 x 63.5 = 1.8161 (g)*
  - *So, the percentage of copper in brass = *$\frac{1.8161}{3.90}\times100$* = 45.567%*
  
    - *Careful: **The questions asks for the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures*

The student is asked to add **A** to samples of **B, C** and **D** in separate test tubes, a **small** amount at a time, until there is no further change. The container of solution **A** has a hazard label.

![q1a-paper-6-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/033-q1a-paper-6-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

i) Identify the hazard indicated by this label.

ii) Describe how you would add small amounts of **A** until there is no further change. Name the apparatus you would use.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The hazard indicated by this label is:

- Corrosive; **[1 mark] **

ii) You would add small amounts of **A** until there is no further change by:

- Drop by drop; **[1 mark] **
- (Dropping) pipette / teat pipette; **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 3 marks] **

- *You can also say corrosive and acidic for part (i) and dropwise / add in drops or you can use a burette for part (ii) *

Identify, by name or formula, the gas produced.

A small amount of this mixture is added to **B** and a white precipitate forms.

Solution **B**

Solution **D**

vi) A concentrated solution of ammonia is added to **B**.

Initially a pale blue precipitate forms. When more ammonia is added, the precipitate dissolves forming a dark blue solution **F**.

Identify, by name or formula, the pale blue precipitate and the species responsible for the dark blue colour in **F**.

**(2)**

vii) A solution of the sodium salt of EDTA, Na<sub>4</sub>EDTA, is added to a sample of solution **F**. The solution turns pale blue.

Write an equation for the reaction. State symbols are not required.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The **formula** of the cation in **B **is:

- Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) / Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub><sup>2+</sup>;** [1 mark] **

ii) The name or formula, the gas produced is:

- Carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2 </sub>(g); **[1 mark] **

iii) The name or formula, of the anion in **C** is:

- Carbonate (ion) / CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> / hydrogencarbonate (ion) / HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>; **[1 mark] **

iv) The name or formula of **A** is:

- (Conc) hydrochloric acid / HCl (aq); **[1 mark] **
- (In (b)(i)) the yellow colour is due to CuCl<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> / tetrachlorocuprate(II); **[1 mark] **

v) Solutions **B **and **D **are:

- (**B**) contains a sulfate ion / SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2‒</sup> / CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) / copper(II) sulphate; **[1 mark] **
- (**D**) is barium chloride (solution) / BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq); **[1 mark] **

vi) The pale blue precipitate and the species responsible for the dark blue colour in **F** is:

- Copper(II) hydroxide / Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) / Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub> (s); **[1 mark]**
- Tetraamminecopper(II) / tetraamminediaquacopper(II) / [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) / [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq); **[1 mark]**

vii) An equation for the reaction is:

- [CuEDTA]<sup>2‒</sup> / CuEDTA<sup>2‒</sup> / Na<sub>2</sub>[CuEDTA] as a product; **[1 mark] **
- Remainder of equation correct; **[1 mark] **

Cu<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4‒</sup> → CuEDTA<sup>2‒</sup>
**   OR**
   Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Na<sub>4</sub>EDTA → CuEDTA<sup>2‒</sup> + 4Na<sup>+</sup>
**   OR**
   [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>((aq))]<sup>2+</sup> + Na<sub>4</sub>EDTA → [CuEDTA]<sup>2‒</sup> + 4Na<sup>+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
**   OR**
   [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>((aq))]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4‒</sup> → [CuEDTA]<sup>2‒</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**Final answer:** **[Total: 11 marks] **

- *For part (i) you can say copper(II) ions or hexaquacopper(II) as your answer *
- *For part (iv) you can say green or tetrachlorocopper ion complex*

  - *This is due to a change in coordination number *
  - *The [Cu(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* complex has a light blue colour*
  - *The [CuCl*<sub>*4*</sub>*]*<sup>*2–*</sup>* has a yellow colour due to the change in the ligand and the change in the coordination number from 6 to 4 *
- *For part (v) you can say barium nitrate / Ba(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* / lead(II) nitrate / Pb(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *For part (vi) you will not gain the mark for [Cu(NH*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq) / hexaaminecopper(II)*
- *This is an example of ligand exchange*

  - *The [Cu(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*6*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* complex has a light blue colour*
  - *The [Cu(NH*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*4*</sub>*(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*<sub>*2*</sub>*]*<sup>*2+*</sup>* has a dark blue colour *

To determine its empirical formula, 1.57 g of the compound was burned completely and the combustion products passed through the apparatus shown.

![q3d-paper-6-2021-june-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/040-q3d-paper-6-2021-june-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

Solid **M** absorbed water and increased in mass by 1.28 g.

Solid **N** absorbed carbon dioxide and increased in mass by 3.14 g.

i) Identify, by name or formula, suitable substances for solids **M** and **N**.

**(2)**

Solid **M** ....................................................................................................... Solid **N** ........................................................................................................

ii) Calculate the **empirical** formula of the compound, using the data given. You **must** show your working.

**(4)**

iii) The mass spectrum of the compound is shown.

![q3d-iii-paper-6-2021-june-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/041-q3d-iii-paper-6-2021-june-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

Deduce the relative molecular mass of the compound, using the mass spectrum.

**(1)**

iv) Deduce the molecular formula of the compound, using your answers to (d)(ii) and (d)(iii).

**(1)**

v) Determine the identity of the compound, using your answer to (d)(iv) and the fragmentation pattern of the mass spectrum. Justify your answer.

**(2)**

![q3dv-paper-6-2021-june-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/042-q3dv-paper-6-2021-june-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)
parts.solution_md:
i)  The identity of solids **M** and **N **are:

- Solid **M**: (anhydrous) calcium chloride / CaCl<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Solid **N**: soda lime / potassium hydroxide / sodium hydroxide / calcium hydroxide / calcium oxide; **[1 mark]**

ii) The **empirical** formula of the compound is:

- Mass of hydrogen = $\frac{2}{18}$ x 1.28 = 0.14222 (g)
**OR**
Moles of hydrogen = $\frac{1.28}{18}$ x 2 = 0.14222 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Mass of carbon = $\frac{12}{44}$ x 3.14 = 0.85636 (g)
**OR**
Moles of carbon (dioxide) = $\frac{3.14}{44}$ = 0.071364 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Mass of oxygen =  1.57 − 0.14222 − 0.85636
= 0.57142 / 0.57 (g)
**OR**
% mass of oxygen = 100 − 9.0587 − 54.545
= 36.396 / 36%; **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

iii) The relative molecular mass of the compound is:

- (*m* / *z* =) 88; **[1 mark]**

iv) The molecular formula of the compound is:

- (x = `fraction numerator M subscript straight r over denominator M subscript straight r space open parentheses straight C subscript 2 straight H subscript 4 straight O close parentheses end fraction space equals space 88 over 44 space equals space 2`) Molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

v) The identity of the compound is:

- Compound** F**; **[1 mark]**
- Justification with reference to both molecular formula / *M*<sub>r</sub> **AND** Fragmentation pattern; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 10 marks]**

- *In part (i), you would have gained marks for the alternatives calcium sulfate, sodium sulfate, magnesium sulfate or silica gel*
- *To find the empirical formula, you need to calculate the mass of each of the elements present*
- *As the products are water and carbon dioxide, the elements present are carbon, hydrogen and oxygen*
- *To find the mass of hydrogen:*

  - *Number of moles of water produced = mass ÷ **M*<sub>*r *</sub>*= 1.28 ÷ 18 = 0.07111 mol*
  - *Number of moles of hydrogen = 2 x moles of water = 2 x 0.07111 = 0.14222 mol*
  - *Mass of hydrogen = 0.14222 x 1 = **0.14222 g*
- *To find the mass of carbon:*

  - *Number of moles of carbon dioxide produced = 3.14 ÷ 44 = 0.071364 mol*
  - *Number of moles of carbon = number of moles of carbon dioxide = 0.071364 mol*
  - *Mass of carbon = 0.071364 x 12 = **0.85636 g*
- *To find the mass of oxygen:*

  - *Mass of oxygen = mass of compound - mass of hydrogen - mass of carbon*
  - *Mass of oxygen = 1.57 - 0.14222 - 0.85636 = **0.57142 g*
- *Once you have calculated the mass of each element, the empirical formula can be found by:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* | > *O* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Divide mass by** A*<sub>*r*</sub> | $\frac{0.85636}{12}\,=0.071363$ | $\frac{0.14222}{1}\,=0.14222$ | $\frac{0.57142}{16}\,=0.035714$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number* | $\frac{0.071363}{0.035714}$ | $\frac{0.14222}{0.035714}$ | $\frac{0.035714}{0.035714}$ |
| > *To give the whole number ratio* | > *2* | > *4* | > *1* |

- *The empirical formula is therefore C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*
- *In part (v), examples of suitable justifications are:*

  - *Peak at **m** / **z** = 29 (for C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>*)*
  *OR*
  *Peak at **m** / **z** = 59 (for COOCH*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>*)*
  *OR*
  *No peak at **m** / **z** = 43 (for CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CO*<sup>*+*</sup>*)*
  *OR*
  *No peak at **m** / **z** = 45 (for C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*OH*<sup>*+*</sup>*)*
  *AND*
  *Molecular formula C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*8*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* / **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 88*
  - *Peak at **m** / **z** = 29 (for C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>*)*
  *AND*
  *D** does not have molecular formula C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*8*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* / **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 88*

parts.problem_md:
Azo dyes, such as Organol Brown, can be made from benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, using the reaction scheme shown.

Due to the toxicity of benzene, the first step is never carried out in a school laboratory.

![q3-paper-6-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/026-q3-paper-6-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

In the preparation of nitrobenzene, benzene is added slowly to a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids.

The mixture is warmed at 55 °C under reflux for 45 minutes. The reaction mixture is stirred continuously.

i) State why a reflux condenser is needed when the mixture is warmed.

**(1)**

ii) Draw a diagram of the apparatus used to warm under reflux in this experiment.

**(3)**

iii) Suggest why the reaction mixture is stirred continuously.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) A reflux condenser is needed when the mixture is warmed

- So that the volatile / toxic benzene doesn’t escape from the reaction mixture; **[1 mark] **

ii) A diagram of the apparatus used to warm under reflux in this experiment is:

![HC6124H0_reflux-apparatus](assets/027-hc6124h0-reflux-apparatus.png)

- Round-bottomed / pear shaped flask containing mixture and heat; **[1 mark] **
- Vertical condenser with water jacket and water flowing in the correct direction; **[1 mark] **
- No gaps and open condenser and apparatus would work; **[1 mark] **

iii) The reaction mixture is stirred continuously because:

- Reactants are immiscible / form separate layers / do not mix; **[1 mark] **
- (The reactants need to be mixed) to ensure enough contact for a reaction to take place; **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 6 marks] **

- *For part (i)*

  - *You can say the reaction reaches completion / otherwise the reaction would not be complete / to ensure all the benzene reacts*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *Any indication of heat including an arrow or water bath or electrical heater will be suitable*
  - *Conical flasks will not be awarded the mark as round bottomed or pear shaped flasks should be used*
  - *You would not get the mark if the condenser and flask are one piece of apparatus, they should be separate with a proper seal shown*
  - *If you drew distillation apparatus you would gain 1 mark  *
  - *When drawing your diagrams double check the joints do not contain gaps as this would mean that any vapours will escape *
- *For part (iii) you can also give the following answers*

  - *Reactants are not completely miscible*
  - *To make the reactants mix*
  - *So it gives a reasonable rate of reaction*
  - *So the reactants come into contact*
  - *So the reactants are exposed to each other*
  - *So the reaction can take place effectively*
  - *To ensure even heat distribution*

Identify a suitable drying agent.
parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md:
Nitrobenzene is then reduced to phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.

Phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid at a temperature between 0 °C and 10 °C to form a diazonium compound.

i) Nitrous acid is formed in the reaction mixture using sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid.

State why nitrous acid is generated in the reaction mixture instead of being obtained from a chemical supplier.

**(1)**

ii) Explain why the temperature of the reaction between phenylamine and nitrous acid must be neither lower than 0 °C nor higher than 10 °C.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) Nitrous acid is generated in the reaction mixture instead of being obtained from a chemical supplier because:

- HNO<sub>2</sub> / nitrous acid is unstable / decomposes (so cannot be transported); **[1 mark] **

ii) The temperature of the reaction between phenylamine and nitrous acid must be neither lower than 0 °C nor higher than 10 °C because:

- Below 0<sup> o</sup>C the reaction is too slow; **[1 mark]**
- Above 10 <sup>o</sup>C the diazonium chloride / compound / ion decomposes / hydrolyses / reacts with water / forms phenol (and nitrogen gas); **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 3 marks] **

- *Nitrous acid is formed 'in situ' *

  - *The phenylamine is first dissolved in hydrochloric acid, and then a solution of sodium or potassium nitrite is added*
  - *The reaction between the hydrochloric acid and the nitrite ions produces the nitrous acid which is a weak acid*
- *You can also say the reaction mixture may solidify or there is less energy for overcoming the activation barrier to gain the first mark*
- *For part (ii) you can say*

  - *Phenol is formed*
  - *The product decomposes*
  - *Phenylamine reacts to form phenol*

parts.problem_md:
Reaction of the diazonium compound with an alkaline solution of naphthalene-1-ol produces the solid azo dye, Organol Brown. The solid is purified by recrystallisation.

Procedure

| Step **1** | The impure Organol Brown is dissolved in a minimum volume of hot solvent. |
|---|---|
| Step **2** | The solution is filtered hot through a preheated funnel. |
| Step **3** | The solution is cooled and filtered using a Buchner funnel. |
| Step **4** | The solid is rinsed with a small amount of ice-cold solvent. |
| Step **5** | The solid is dried in a desiccator. |

i) State why a **minimum** volume of hot solvent is used in Step **1**.

**(1)**

ii) Explain why a preheated funnel is used in Step **2**.

**(1)**

iii) Give a reason for each of the two filtrations in Steps **2** and **3**.

**(2)**

iv) Give a possible reason why it is preferable to dry the solid in a desiccator rather than in an oven in Step **5**.

**(1)**
parts.solution_md:
i) A **minimum** volume of hot solvent is used in Step **1 **because:

- (So a lot of the azo dye) does not remain in solution (when it cools) 
**OR** 
Gives a saturated solution (when it has cooled);** [1 mark] **

ii) A preheated funnel is used in Step **2 **because:

- (Pre-heated) to prevent (premature) crystallisation (of the azo dye in the funnel); **[1 mark] **

iii) A reason for each of the two filtrations in Steps **2** and **3 **is:

- Step **2** is to remove insoluble impurities; **[1 mark] **
- Step **3** is to remove soluble impurities; **[1 mark] **

iv) A possible reason why it is preferable to dry the solid in a desiccator rather than in an oven in Step **5 **is:

- To avoid (thermal) decomposition; **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 5 marks] **

- *For part (i) saying ‘to obtain a concentrated solution’ or 'to maximise yield' will not score the mark, be specific with your answers *

  - *When recrystallising you will always use the minimum amount of solvent*
- *For part (ii) you can say to keep the Organol Brown / product / solid in solution*
- *For part (iii) if you wrote ‘to remove insoluble and soluble impurities’ you would score 1 mark *
- *For part (iv) avoid melting the dye or crystals are acceptable answers*

The melting temperature of the recrystallised Organol Brown is measured to check its purity.

State what you would observe if the sample was pure.
parts.solution_md:
If the sample was pure you would see a:

- Sharp melting temperature;** [1 mark] **

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Saying melting would occur over a small range, for example ±2 *<sup>*o*</sup>*C would gain you the mark*
- *The question makes reference to what you would see if the sample was **pure*

parts.solution_md:
**Two** reasons why gloves should be worn in Step **1** are:

- (Concentrated hydrochloric) acid is <u>corrosive</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You are given enough information to answer this question*
- *The preparation of phenylamine uses:*

  - *Concentrated hydrochloric acid which is corrosive*
  - *Nitrobenzene which is toxic by skin absorption*

- *Extra marking points about incorrect / irrelevant answers include:*

  - *Hydrochloric acid is toxic / harmful*
  - *Any comments about granulated tin or glass are ignored*
  - *Nitrobenzene is corrosive does not gain any marks, as it is not*

parts.problem_md:
i) State the role of tin in the preparation.

**(1)**

ii) Suggest, by name or formula, the identity of the initial precipitate formed in Step **3**.

**(1)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The role of tin in the preparation is:

- A reducing agent / reductant; **[1 mark]**

ii) The identity of the initial precipitate formed in Step **3** is:

- Tin(IV) hydroxide / Sn(OH)<sub>4</sub>
**OR**
Tin(II) hydroxide / Sn(OH)<sub>2</sub>
**OR**
Tin hydroxide; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The tin causes the nitrobenzene to be reduced so it is a reducing agent*

  - *This happens due to the oxidation reactions of tin: Sn → Sn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* + 2e*<sup>*–*</sup>*  Sn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* → Sn*<sup>*4+*</sup>* + 2e*<sup>*–*</sup>* *
- *The tin ions formed during these oxidation reactions are able to react with the excess sodium hydroxide resulting in the formation of a mixture of tin(II) hydroxide and tin(IV) hydroxide*

  - *Sn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* + 2OH*<sup>*–*</sup>* → Sn(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *Sn*<sup>*4+*</sup>* + 2OH*<sup>*–*</sup>* → Sn(OH)*<sub>*4*</sub>* *

parts.problem_md: State why the distillate in Step **4** is cloudy.
parts.solution_md:
The distillate in Step **4** is cloudy because:

- The water contains phenylamine / the phenylamine contains water
**OR** Phenylamine and water are partially miscible
**OR**
The distillate is an emulsion; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *During steam distillation, steam is bubbled through the reaction mixture *
- *As the steam bubbles through the reaction mixture, the phenylamine is distilled along with the water (from the steam)*
- *This results in a cloudy distillate as phenylamine is not miscible / is only partially miscible in water*
- *One of the most common incorrect answers is about the distillate containing impurities*

  - *This is incorrect as steam distillation is a technique used to purify mixtures of liquids *

parts.problem_md: Suggest why sodium chloride is added to the distillate in Step **5**.
parts.solution_md:
Sodium chloride is added to the distillate in Step **5** to:

- Aid separation (of the layers)
**OR** Decrease the solubility of phenylamine (in the aqueous layer)
**OR**
To cause the phenylamine to salt / crash out
**OR**
Increase the density of the aqueous layer; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The sodium chloride aids separation by increasing the density of the aqueous layer causing the phenylamine to "salt" into the organic layer*
- *The reason for the addition is not well known with examiners commenting that it appears many students have not performed this practical *

parts.problem_md:
i) Draw a **labelled** diagram of the separating funnel **at the end** of Step **5**.

**(2)**

ii) State how you would relieve the pressure in the separating funnel in Step **5**.

**(1)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The **labelled** diagram of the separating funnel **at the end** of Step **5** is:

![sep-funnel](assets/024-sep-funnel.png)

- Diagram of a separating funnel; **[1 mark]**
- Two layers with the lower layer labelled aqueous 
**AND **
The upper layer labelled organic; **[1 mark]**

ii) The pressure in the separating funnel is relieved by:

- Inverting (the funnel) 
**AND **
**o**pening the tap 
**OR**
Removing the stopper; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Although this reaction may not be familiar, you are still expected to know how to use a separating funnel*
- *You are given the density information to determine whether the organic layer is the top or bottom layer*

  - *The density of ether is 0.71 g cm*<sup>*-3*</sup>* This means that it is less dense than water and the top layer will, therefore, be the organic layer*

parts.problem_md: Suggest **one** reason for adding pellets of potassium hydroxide in Step **6**.
parts.solution_md:
**One** reason for adding pellets of potassium hydroxide in Step **6** is:

- Potassium hydroxide / it is a drying agent  
**OR **
Potassium hydroxide / it removes water; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Careful:** Do not be put off by the fact that the potassium hydroxide is not explicitly described as anhydrous *

  - *Potassium hydroxide is still a drying agent*
- *Most incorrect answers were about neutralisation, suggesting that students saw hydroxide and guessed at a reaction that they know hydroxides do*

parts.problem_md: State how the mixture would be heated to distil off the ether in Step** 7**. Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
To distil  off the ether, the mixture could be:

- Heated in a water bath 
**OR **
Heated with an electrical heater; **[1 mark]**
- (Because,) ether / it is (highly) flammable
**OR **
(Because,) ether / it will catch fire; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You are told that ether is flammable at the start of this overall question*
- *Therefore, your answer has to consider this fact and suggest an appropriate method of heating*

parts.problem_md:
Calculate the mass of phenylamine formed in this preparation.

The limiting reagent is nitrobenzene and the overall yield by mass is 43%.

Refer to all the information at the start of the question.
parts.solution_md:
The mass of phenylamine formed in this preparation is:

- Mass of nitrobenzene = 2.52 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of nitrobenzene = 0.020488 **OR **2.0488 x 10<sup>-2</sup>; **[1 mark]**

Plus **one **of the following:

Option 1:

- Moles of phenylamine for a 43% yield = 0.0088098 **OR** 8.8098 x 10<sup>-3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of phenylamine product = 0.8193 (g); **[1 mark]**

Option 2:

- Mass of phenylamine for a 100% yield = 1.9054 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Mass of phenylamine product = 0.8193 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To calculate the mass of nitrobenzene, use mass = density x volume*

  - *Mass of nitrobenzene = 1.20 x 2.1 = 2.52 g*
- *To calculate the moles of nitrobenzene, use moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

  - *Moles of nitrobenzene = *$\frac{2.52}{123.0}$* = 0.020488 **OR **2.0488 x 10*<sup>*-2*</sup>* *
- * From the chemical equation, 1 mole of nitrobenzene forms 1 mole of phenylamine*

  - *So the moles of phenylamine = 0.020488 **OR **2.0488 x 10*<sup>*-2*</sup>* *
- *With a 43% yield, the moles of phenylamine = 0.020488 x *$\frac{43}{100}$* = 0.0088098 **OR** 8.8098 x 10*<sup>*-3*</sup>* *
- *To calculate the mass of the phenylamine product, use mass = moles x **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* *

  - *So the mass of the phenylamine product = 0.0088098 x 93.0 = 0.8913 g*
- *If you make a mistake in any of the steps, you can still continue using your incorrect value in the subsequent steps and gain marks by transferred error*

This question is about the alkaline hydrolysis of an ester, **X**. **X** is an alkyl benzoate and can be represented by the formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOR, where R is the alkyl group. The equation for the hydrolysis is

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOR + NaOH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa + ROH

**Procedure**

|---|---|
| Step **2** | Heat the flask and contents under reflux for 20 minutes. |
| Step **3** | Allow the apparatus to cool and then rearrange it for distillation. Distil the mixture and collect about 2 cm<sup>3</sup>of the alcohol ROH. |
| Step **4** | Allow the pear-shaped flask to cool, pour the contents into a beaker and add excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Impure benzoic acid forms as crystals in the mixture. |
| Step **5** | Recrystallise the benzoic acid using water as the solvent. |
| Step **6** | Weigh the dry crystals and determine their melting temperature. |

parts.problem_md:

Describe a **chemical** test, and its positive result, to show the presence of an –OH group in **any** alcohol.
parts.solution_md:
A **chemical** test, and its positive result, to show the presence of an –OH group in **any** alcohol is:

Any **one **of the following:

parts.problem_md:
i) Write an equation for the reaction taking place in Step **4**. Use structural formulae for the organic substances. State symbols are not required.

**(1)**

ii) State what should be done to separate the benzoic acid from the mixture produced in Step **4**, before carrying out Step **5**.

**(1)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The equation for the reaction taking place in Step **4**, using structural formulae for the organic substances, is:

Any **one** of the following:

- C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH + NaCl; **[1 mark]**
- C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa + H<sup>+</sup> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH + Na<sup>+</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH; **[1 mark]**
- C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH + Cl<sup>−</sup>; **[1 mark]**

ii) To separate the benzoic acid from the mixture produced in Step **4**, you should:

**OR**
Filtration under reduced pressure / with a Buchner flask
**OR**
A diagram showing filtration; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The equation at the start of the question tells you that you are making C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*COONa + ROH*
  - *Step **3** tells you the ROH has been distilled off, which leaves the C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*COONa in the pear-shaped flask*

- *The preparation of benzoic acid is similar to aspirin preparation in terms of the main steps*

  - *Filtration*

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Examiners like to ask about recrystallization because there are some key points that have to happen / that the examiners are looking for:*

parts.problem_md:
The molar mass of **X**, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOR, is 178 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.

i) Deduce the formula of the alkyl group, R.

**(1)**

ii)  Use your answer to (f)(i) to draw the structures of the four possible alcohols, ROH.

**(2)**

|   |   |
|---|---|
|   |   |

iii) The part of the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of **X** corresponding to the R group contains only two peaks. 
Deduce the structure of** X.**

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The formula of the alkyl group, R, is:

- C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>; **[1 mark]**

ii) The structures of the four possible alcohols, ROH, are:

![c4h9oh-isomers](assets/030-c4h9oh-isomers.png)

- **Two** or **three** alcohols correct; **[1 mark]**

iii) The structure of** X** is:

![t-butyl-benzoate](assets/031-t-butyl-benzoate.png)

- The structure of any butyl benzoate; **[1 mark]**
- Tertiary butyl / t-butyl group; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The question tells you that the molar mass of X, C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*COOR, is 178 g mol*<sup>*−1*</sup>* *
  - *This means that R = 178 – C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*COO = 178 - 121 = 57 g mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>* *
  - *The 57 g mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>* must be made of carbon and hydrogen atoms, which leads to C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*9*</sub>* *

  - *This results in the t-butyl / –C(CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*3*</sub>* group and gives the final correct answer shown in the mark scheme*

parts.problem_md:
A student investigates the properties of copper(II) bisglycinate, [Cu(gly)<sub>2</sub>], where gly represents the glycinate ion, H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>.

The student dissolves [Cu(gly)<sub>2</sub>] in dilute sulfuric acid to decompose the complex, releasing Cu<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) and glycine, H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>COOH (aq). The resulting solution is divided into portions for the tests below.

Complete the table to show the expected observations when each reagent is added to a separate portion of the decomposed solution.

| Reagent added | Expected observation |
|---|---|
| A few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, then excess |   |
| Excess ammonia solution |   |
parts.solution_md:
| Reagent added | Expected observation | |---|---| | A few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, then excess | Blue / light blue / pale blue precipitate / ppt / solid forms initially **[1 mark]**

The precipitate remains / does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide solution **[1 mark]** | | Excess ammonia solution | Blue / light blue / pale blue precipitate / ppt / solid forms initially **[1 mark]**

The precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep / royal / dark blue solution **[1 mark]** | > **[mark-scheme]** > The colour **AND **precipitate / ppt / solid are both required > > The blue precipitate must be described as blue, light blue or pale blue. Any reference to the blue precipitate being deep blue, royal blue or dark blue is not accepted > **[exam-tip]** > The colour matters: > > - Blue, light blue, and pale blue are the correct colours for the precipitate formed with Cu2+ ions. > - Deep blue, royal blue or dark blue are the correct colours for the solution formed when excess ammonia dissolves the precipitate. > > Always include "precipitate", "solid", or "ppt" alongside the colour. > > - Just "the solution turns blue" does not describe a solid forming, which means it get no marks. > > Even though the question states *excess* ammonia is added, examiners expect you to describe the entire visual sequence. This means that you must state that a blue precipitate initially forms and then dissolves to a deep blue solution to achieve both marks.

parts.problem_md: Give the formula of the complex ion formed when excess ammonia solution is added to the Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) solution.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The formula of the complex ion formed when excess ammonia solution is added to the Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) solution is:
> 
> - [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>
> **OR**
> [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Square brackets are not required for the mark
> 
> State symbols are ignored
> 
> If a chemical name is also given, then it must be correct:
> 
> - [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> = tetraamminediaquacopper(II)
> - [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> tetraamminecopper(II)
> 
> [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> A very common mistake is to write [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> In aqueous solution, only four of the six water ligands on Cu<sup>2+</sup> are displaced by ammonia. The remaining two coordination sites are occupied by water molecules. So, the correct formula is:
> 
> [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> Copper(II) remains six-coordinate overall, but ammonia only partially substitutes the water

parts.problem_md:
A student suggests adding phosphorus(V) chloride to a separate portion of the decomposed aqueous solution to confirm the presence of a functional group in glycine.

i) State the observation the student would expect to make if this functional group were present.

[1]

ii) Explain why this test is invalid for confirming the structure of glycine in this specific mixture.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The student would observe:
> 
> - Steamy / misty / white fumes **[1 mark]**
> 
> "White smoke" is not accepted
> 
> ii) This test is invalid because:
> 
> - The mixture is aqueous / contains water **AND** water reacts with PCl<sub>5</sub> (to produce the same misty fumes) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question is testing a skill that catches most students out: spotting when a standard test fails because of the conditions it is being applied in, not because of the target compound.
> 
> PCl<sub>5</sub> reacts vigorously with water to produce hydrogen chloride gas (misty fumes).
> 
> The solution is aqueous because dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> was used to decompose the complex. This means that misty fumes will be seen regardless of what organic compound is present.
> 
> - The water alone is enough to give this result
> - So, the observation tells you nothing reliable about the structure of glycine.
> 
> To score the mark, your answer must include both parts: state that water is present **AND** state that water reacts with PCl<sub>5</sub> to produce the same misty fumes. Saying only that "the test is unreliable" or only that "water is present" is not enough.
> 
> The general principle is that whenever a question asks you to evaluate a proposed test, ask two questions:
> 
> 1. Does the test actually detect what is claimed?
> 2. Is there anything else in the mixture that could give the same result
> 
> - In PCl<sub>5</sub> questions, water is almost always the answer to question 2.

parts.problem_md: State which functional group in glycine the PCl<sub>5</sub> test was intended to confirm.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The glycine functional group is:
> 
> - Carboxylic acid / −COOH / −CO<sub>2</sub>H 
> **OR**
> Hydroxyl / −OH group **[1 mark]**
> 
> "OH group" without the preceding bond, e.g. "-OH", is not accepted
> 
> "OH<sup>-</sup>" and hydroxide are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> PCl<sub>5</sub> reacts with hydroxyl / –OH groups.
> 
> In glycine, the –OH group is part of the carboxylic acid (–COOH). Although carboxylic acid and hydroxyl group are both accepted, carboxylic acid / –COOH is the more precise answer.

parts.problem_md:
A student adds excess sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to a separate portion of the decomposed solution.

i) State the observation the student would make.

[1]

ii) Explain why this test does not confirm that glycine contains a carboxylic acid group.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The observation would be:
> 
> - Effervescence / fizzing / bubbles **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Gas evolves', 'gas is given off' and 'gas is produced' are not accepted
> 
> ii) This test does not confirm that glycine contains a carboxylic acid group because:
> 
> - The sodium hydrogencarbonate would also react with the sulfuric acid (to produce CO<sub>2</sub>) 
> **OR**
> Sulfuric acid also gives a positive result **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you are asked for observations, you need to answer with something you can detect with your senses. For this reaction:
> 
> - You can see fizzing
> - You cannot see carbon dioxide gas being produced
> 
> Gas being produced is a conclusion being drawn from the fizzing observation
> 
> This question uses the NaHCO<sub>3</sub> to test for the glycine −COOH group. However, the student decomposed the original copper complex using dilute sulfuric acid. Sulfuric acid is a strong acid, which will result in vigorous effervescence when sodium hydrogencarbonate is added. This means that there is another false positive regardless of the glycine -COOH group

parts.problem_md:
Explain why the same observation would **not** be seen if phenol were used instead of the decomposed solution.

Refer to acid strength in your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid / H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
> **OR**
> Phenol is a weaker acid than carboxylic acids / glycine **[1 mark]**
> - Phenol is therefore not strong enough to react with / protonate HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> / sodium hydrogencarbonate
> **OR**
> Phenol cannot donate H<sup>+</sup> to HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> / cannot displace CO<sub>2</sub> from HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Phenol is a weak acid" without a comparison to carbonic acid or carboxylic acids is not accepted
> 
> Answers that do not reference acid strength cannot score either mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key phrase in the question is "refer to acid strength", which means that a comparison is needed.
> 
> Saying "phenol is a weak acid" on its own scores zero for the first mark, because it does not explain why phenol fails to react with HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>.
> 
> The acid strength ordering to remember here is:
> 
> - Carboxylic acids (p*K*<sub>a</sub> approximately 4–5)
> 
>   - Stronger than carbonic acid
> - Carbonic acid (p*K*<sub>a1</sub> approximately 6.4)
> 
>   - The boundary: acids stronger than this can protonate HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>
> - Phenol (p*K*<sub>a</sub> approximately 10)
> 
>   - Weaker than carbonic acid, so cannot protonate HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>
> 
> For HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> to be protonated and release CO<sub>2</sub>, the acid providing the proton must be stronger than carbonic acid. Carboxylic acids are strong enough but phenol is not. Although both contain an O–H bond, the difference is how readily they release the proton.

parts.problem_md:
The student wants to determine if the original solid copper(II) bisglycinate complex contained any sulfate (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>) ions as an impurity.

They add a few drops of aqueous barium chloride (BaCl<sub>2</sub>) to a portion of the decomposed solution and observe a white precipitate. The student concludes that the original complex contained a sulfate impurity.

Criticise this conclusion.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The conclusion is invalid 
> **OR**
> The white precipitate does not prove the complex contained sulfate ions **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> was used to decompose the complex / introduces SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions into the solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that suggest the white precipitate is anything other than barium sulfate / BaSO<sub>4</sub> are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an evaluation question.
> 
> The observation is real as a white precipitate does form. But, the conclusion is invalid because the student has not accounted for what was done at the start of the experiment.
> 
> Dilute sulfuric acid was used in part (a) to decompose the complex. This introduces SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions directly into the solution. When BaCl<sub>2</sub> is added, those SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions precipitate as BaSO<sub>4</sub> regardless of whether the original complex contained any sulfate at all.
> 
> The white precipitate proves only that BaSO<sub>4</sub> has formed. It does not prove that the original complex was contaminated with sulfate. This is a false positive caused by the choice of acid used in the decomposition step.
> 
> To score both marks, your answer needs two things:
> 
> - State that the conclusion is invalid / the test has a flaw
> - Identify the specific source of SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions — the sulfuric acid used in part (a)

parts.problem_md:
A student prepares aspirin by heating salicylic acid with excess ethanoic anhydride. The reaction is carried out under reflux.

Give one reason why reflux is used rather than heating the mixture in an open beaker.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Reflux is used because:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - To prevent the escape / loss / evaporation of (volatile / flammable) reactants / products
> **OR**
> To prevent the evaporation of ethanoic anhydride / salicylic acid / aspirin / ethanoic acid
> - To allow the mixture to be heated for a period of time without boiling dry
> - To ensure the reaction goes to completion.
> - So the volatile gases condense and return to the flask
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answer about reducing or preventing spillages, bubbling over and explosions are not accepted
> 
> "Chemicals are toxic" is not an accepted answer unless it is specifically linked to the escape of volatile vapours.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reflux keeps volatile substances in the reaction mixture by condensing their vapours and returning them to the flask. The condenser does not cool the reaction . The mixture still heats at its boiling point and the condenser simply prevents anything from escaping.
> 
> The most common incorrect answers are:
> 
> - "To prevent spillages / stop the liquid bubbling over"
> 
>   - Stopping liquid from physically splashing out is the job of a larger flask or anti-bumping granules, not a condenser.
> - "To increase the rate of reaction / to heat the mixture"
> 
>   - Heating in an open beaker would also raise the temperature.
> 
> The question asks specifically why reflux is used instead of an open beaker. So, your answer must talk about how the condenser returns the volatile vapour to the flask
> 
> A useful way to remember the difference between reflux and distillation is:
> 
> - In reflux, you want the vapour to go back into the flask
> - In distillation, you want to collect it.
> 
> Same condenser, different purpose.

parts.problem_md:
After heating under reflux, the student pours the reaction mixture into a beaker of iced water.

Give **one** reason for adding iced water at this stage.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A reason for adding iced water is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - To react with / remove / hydrolyse the excess ethanoic anhydride
> - To dissolve excess ethanoic anhydride / ethanoic acid
> - To precipitate / crystallise the aspirin (as it is less soluble in cold water)
> - To improve the yield of crystals
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> "To quench / stop the reaction" is not accepted
> 
> Just "to cool the mixture down" is not accepted unless specifically linked to the formation of crystals

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark is awarded for any one valid reason — either what the water does chemically (reacting with excess ethanoic anhydride) or what the cold temperature does physically (causing aspirin to crystallise out of solution).
> 
> Two answers that do not score:
> 
> - "To quench / stop the reaction" — the reaction is already complete; the water destroys the excess ethanoic anhydride rather than stopping the main reaction
> - Just "to cool the mixture down" — this only scores if you link it explicitly to the crystallisation or precipitation of aspirin

parts.problem_md:
The student filters the solid aspirin from the mixture.

Name the apparatus used to filter the product rapidly under reduced pressure.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The apparatus used to filter the product rapidly under reduced pressure is:
> 
> - Büchner / Hirsch / suction / vacuum funnel (and flask) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Phonetic spellings of Büchner are accepted, e.g. Buchner
> 
> "Filter funnel" or just "funnel" are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Büchner funnel has a flat, perforated base. It connects to a side-arm flask (Büchner flask), and reduced pressure created by a water pump or vacuum draws the liquid through the filter paper much faster than gravity alone. This is the standard method for isolating a solid product quickly and with minimal loss.
> 
> The most common error students make is just writing "a funnel and filter paper". This is not accepted because it implies standard gravity filtration.

parts.problem_md:
The crude aspirin is recrystallised by dissolving it in the minimum volume of hot solvent and allowing the solution to cool.

Explain why the **minimum** volume of hot solvent is used.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The minimum volume of hot solvent is used because:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - It forms a saturated solution (so that crystals form on cooling)
> - So that the minimum amount of aspirin / product remains in solution (when it cools)
> - To ensure crystallisation occurs
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> "To maximise yield" and "to obtain a concentrated solution" are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark requires an explanation of the mechanism, not just the outcome. The key idea is that using the minimum volume creates a saturated solution at the boiling point. When it cools, the solubility drops and crystals are forced out of solution.
> 
> If you use too much solvent, the solution will not be saturated when it cools, meaning more aspirin stays dissolved and less crystallises out.
> 
> Answers like "to maximise yield" or "to get a concentrated solution" gain no marks as they describe the goal or an observation. They do not describe the physical chemistry behind why the minimum volume achieves it.

parts.problem_md:
The student measures the melting point of the recrystallised product and records a melting range of 120–128 °C. The melting point of pure aspirin is 135 °C.

State **two** ways in which the student's data shows that the recrystallised product is impure.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The data shows  that the recrystallised product is impure because:
> 
> - The melting temperature / it is lower (than the data book value / 135 °C) **[1 mark]**
> - It melts over a range of temperatures / it melts over an 8 °C range **OR**
> The melting temperature is not sharp **[1 mark]**
> 
> Any use of "boiling temperature" or "boiling point" instead of melting temperature means that the first mark cannot be scored
> 
> Vague answers like "the temperature is inaccurate" are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Pure compounds melt sharply at a single temperature (or over a very narrow range of 1–2 °C). Two features here indicate impurity:
> 
> - A broad melting range (8 °C, from 120 to 128 °C)
> - A melting point below the literature value for pure aspirin (135 °C)
> 
> Both occur because impurities disrupt the regular crystal lattice, requiring less energy to overcome. So, the product melts at a lower temperature and over a wider range.

parts.problem_md:
The student records the IR spectrum of the recrystallised product. In addition to the absorptions expected for pure aspirin, a sharp absorption is observed at 3550 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

The table shows relevant IR absorption ranges.

| Bond | Wavenumber range / cm<sup>−1</sup> |
|---|---|
| O–H (phenol, free) | 3750–3200 |
| O–H (carboxylic acid, broad) | 3300–2500 |
| C=O (ester) | 1750–1735 |
| C=O (carboxylic acid) | 1725–1700 |

Identify the bond responsible for the absorption at 3550 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the functional group in which this bond appears in the impurity.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond responsible for the absorption at 3550 cm<sup>−1</sup> is:
> 
> - O–H bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> The functional group is:
> 
> - Phenol / phenolic O–H / –OH group in a phenol **[1 mark]**
> 
> "C-OH" or "hydroxide" are not accepted for the first mark
> 
> Just "hydroxyl group" without specifying phenol is not accepted for the second mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are two types of O–H absorption in the IR spectrum:
> 
> - Carboxylic acid O–H: broad, 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>
> - Phenol O–H: sharper, 3750–3200 cm<sup>−1</sup>
> 
> The absorption at 3550 cm<sup>−1</sup> falls in the phenol O–H range. Both aspirin and salicylic acid contain a carboxylic acid O–H.
> 
> So, the carboxylic acid O–H cannot distinguish them.
> 
> The phenol O–H at 3550 cm<sup>−1</sup> is the distinguishing absorption.
> 
> Examiners also comment that some students suggest the impurity is water, since it wasn't dried properly. Water does absorb in this region, but the question explicitly asks for the functional group in the impurity. This implies an organic functional group from an unreacted starting material.

parts.problem_md: Identify the impurity in the product. Explain, with reference to the structures of aspirin and the impurity, why the absorption at 3550 cm<sup>−1</sup> is not present in the spectrum of pure aspirin.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The impurity is:
> 
> - Salicylic acid / 2-hydroxybenzoic acid 
> **OR**
> (Unreacted) reactant / starting material **[1 mark]**

> 
> - The phenol / phenolic O–H group (in salicylic acid) has been converted into an ester

Write the **ionic** equation for the conversion of  $\mathrm{VO}_{3}^{-}$ to $\mathrm{VO}_{2}^{+}$ on the addition of dilute sulfuric acid. State symbols are not required.

ii) State the colour of an **acidified** solution of ammonium vanadate(V).

The student suggested that the sequence of colours observed could be explained by the presence of the vanadium species shown in the table.

**OR**
The initial green is due to a mixture of +5 and +4 oxidation states / mixture of yellow and blue; **[1 mark]**

- Oxidation of vanadium (from +2 to +3) by oxygen / O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen / O<sub>2</sub> isn’t a strong enough oxidising agent to oxidise vanadium(III) (under these conditions); **[1 mark]**

  - *Oxidation to +4 / +5 is too slow*
  - *Any indication that no further oxidation (of +3) occurs e.g. V*<sup>*3+*</sup>* ions are harder to oxidise*

parts.problem_md:
In Method 2, 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of potassium chlorate(V) was mixed with 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.0750 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> of iron(II) sulfate. The iron (II) sulfate was in excess.

The whole of this solution required 9.25 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.050 mol dm<sup>–3 </sup>of potassium manganate(VII) to completely react.

The equations for the reactions are

$\mathrm{ClO}_{3}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+6\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+6H^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+6\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})+3H_{2}O(l)\,\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+5\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+8H^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\rightarrow\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+5\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})+4H_{2}O(l)$

Calculate the concentration, in mol dm<sup>–3</sup>, of the potassium chlorate(V) solution. You **must** show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the concentration, in mol dm<sup>–3</sup>, of the potassium chlorate(V) solution.

- Calculation of initial number of moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> $\frac{150}{1000}$ × 0.0750 = 0.01125 / 1.125 × 10<sup>-2</sup> (mol) (answer 1); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of the number of moles of potassium manganate(VII) in titration $\frac{9.25}{1000}$ × 0.050 = 0.0004625 / 4.625 × 10<sup>-4</sup> (mol) (answer 2);** [1 mark]**
- Calculation of the number of moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> remaining after the reactions (answer 2) × 5 = 0.0023125 / 2.3125 × 10<sup>-3</sup> (mol) (answer 3); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of the number of moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> that have reacted (answer 1) – (answer 3) 0.01125 – 0.0023125 = 0.0089375 / 8.9375 × 10<sup>-3</sup> (mol) (answer 4); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of the number of moles of chlorate ions that have reacted $\frac{(\mathrm{answer}4)}{6}$ $\frac{0.008375}{6}$ = 0.0014895833 / 1.48958 × 10<sup>-3</sup> (mol) (answer 5); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of the concentration of the solution `fraction numerator open parentheses answer space 5 close parentheses over denominator 0.050 end fraction`  $\frac{0.0014895833}{0.050}$= 0.0297917 / 2.97917 × 10<sup>-2</sup>;** [1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 6 marks] **

- *Remember:** moles = concentration x volume (dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) and concentration = *`fraction numerator moles over denominator volume space open parentheses dm cubed close parentheses end fraction`
- *If you are stuck at the start of a calculation then the best thing to do is calculate the number of moles of what you have been given*

  - *Notice there are 2 marks for calculating the number of moles of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* ions and potassium manganate(VII) *
- *Read the question carefully and look for key phrases like 'excess' which will tell you more information *
- *Use the ratios in the equations:*

$\mathrm{ClO}_{3}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+6\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+6H^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+6\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})+3H_{2}O(l)\,\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+5\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+8H^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\rightarrow\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+5\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})+4H_{2}O(l)$

- *The number of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* ions remaining in solution will be 5 times the amount of MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*-*</sup>* ions as it is a 5:1 ratio*
- *Therefore the number of moles of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* that have reacted can be subtracted from the initially calculated moles of excess Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* *
- *Finally, as it is a 6:1 ratio of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* to ClO*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*-*</sup>* ions, you must now divide this answer by 6 to get the number of moles of ClO*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*-*</sup>* ions, then you can find the concentration of the potassium chlorate(V) solution *

parts.problem_md:
A student determines the percentage by mass of iron in iron tablets by titrating iron(II) ions from the dissolved tablets with potassium manganate(VII) solution.

The equation for the reaction is:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq) + 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Each tablet also contains citric acid as a binder. Citric acid does not react with potassium manganate(VII).

State the observation at the endpoint of the titration.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The observation is:
> 
> - The solution turns / stays pink 
> **OR**
> There is a permanent pink colour / a pink colour that does not decolourise on standing **[1 mark]**
> 
> Pink or pale pink are accepted for the mark
> 
> Purple or shades of purple are not accepted answers
> 
> If a complete colour change is given, then the starting colour must be correct, e.g. from colourless to pink

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this titration, KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution is added from the burette into the colourless Fe<sup>2+</sup> solution in the conical flask.
> 
> Each addition temporarily turns the solution purple, but this rapidly decolourises as Fe<sup>2+</sup> reduces MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> to Mn<sup>2+</sup> (colourless).
> 
> At the endpoint, the last drop of KMnO<sub>4</sub> is not immediately decolourised. So, the solution remains a permanent pale pink.

parts.problem_md:
The student acidifies the iron(II) solution with dilute sulfuric acid before adding potassium manganate(VII).

Explain why dilute sulfuric acid is used to acidify the solution rather than dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute nitric acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Chloride ions / Cl<sup>−</sup> would be oxidised by / react with MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> / potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub> would oxidise iron(II) / Fe<sup>2+</sup> to iron(III) / Fe<sup>3+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow "HCl forms Cl<sub>2</sub> gas" for the first mark
> 
> Allow "nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent" for the second mark
> 
> Chlorine ions are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks for two separate reasons — one for each acid.
> 
> Hydrochloric acid is not used because Cl<sup>−</sup> ions are oxidised by MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> to Cl<sub>2</sub>. This consumes extra KMnO<sub>4</sub> beyond what is needed to oxidise Fe<sup>2+</sup>, making the titre too large and the calculated iron content too high.
> 
> Nitric acid is not used because it is an oxidising acid. It would oxidise Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup> before the titration begins, reducing the amount of Fe<sup>2+</sup> available to react with KMnO<sub>4</sub>. The titre would be too small and the calculated iron content would be too low.
> 
> Dilute sulfuric acid provides the 8H<sup>+</sup> ions required per MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> ion (see the equation in the stem), and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions are not oxidised by KMnO<sub>4</sub> and do not interfere with Fe<sup>2+</sup>, so no side reactions occur.

parts.solution_md:
To calculate the percentage by mass of iron in each tablet:

- Calculate moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> used:

moles = concentration x volume (dm<sup>3</sup>)

moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 0.00500 × `open parentheses fraction numerator 18.50 over denominator 1000 end fraction close parentheses`

moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 9.25 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Determine the moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot:

  - From the equation, 1 mole of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq) reacts with 5 moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in aliquot = 5 × 9.25 × 10<sup>−5</sup>

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in aliquot = 4.625 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol

- Scale up to find moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> solution:

total moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> = 4.625 × 10<sup>−4</sup> × `open parentheses fraction numerator 250.0 over denominator 25.0 end fraction close parentheses`

total moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> = 4.625 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass of Fe in all 6 tablets:

mass = moles x *A*<sub>r</sub>

mass of Fe in 6 tablets = 4.625 × 10<sup>−3</sup> × 55.8

mass of Fe in 6 tablets = 0.2581 g

- Calculate the mass of Fe in 1 tablet:

mass of Fe per tablet = $\frac{0.2581}{6}$

mass of Fe per tablet = 0.04302 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage by mass of iron:

percentage by mass of iron = $\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{iron} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{tablet}}{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{tablet}}$ x 100

percentage by mass of iron = $\frac{0.04302}{0.380}$× 100

percentage by mass of iron = **11.3%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly calculating the number of moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> (9.25 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol)
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> solution (4.625 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol)
> 
> 1 mark for correctly calculating the mass of Fe per tablet (0.04302 g)
> 
> 1 mark for correctly calculating the percentage of iron (11.3%)
> 
> Correct answer with no working shown scores 4 marks
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect titre in part (c) and throughout. One error incurs one mark deduction, regardless of how far it propagates

> **[exam-tip]**
> You need to plan your route through this calculation before writing anything. The five steps are:
> 
> 1. Moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> from titre and concentration
> 2. Moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot using the 1:5 ratio
> 3. Moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the full 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> solution (×10 scale factor)
> 4. Mass of Fe per tablet (total mass ÷ 6)
> 5. Percentage by mass (mass of Fe per tablet ÷ 0.380 × 100)
> 
> There are three traps, which cost one mark each:
> 
> 1. The stoichiometry trap
> 
>   - The equation shows 1 MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> reacts with 5 Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
>   - You must multiply moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> by 5 to get moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
> 2. The scale factor trap
> 
>   - The titre gave you the moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in a 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot, not in the whole flask.
>   - The 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> volumetric flask is ten times larger, so you must multiply by 10.
> 3. The six tablets trap
> 
>   - This catches the strongest students.
>   - The total mass of iron in the 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> solution came from dissolving six tablets, not one.
>   - You must divide by 6 to get the mass of Fe per tablet before calculating the percentage.
> 
> Error carried forward:
> 
> One error costs one mark, regardless of how far it propagates. So even if you make one of the mistakes above, keep working as you can still score three out of four. This is why you should always show your working

The graph below shows the pH curve obtained when sodium hydroxide solution is added to an aqueous solution of the citric acid released from the tablets.

![Graph showing pH versus volume of NaOH in cm³. pH rises sharply around 25 cm³, indicating a titration curve with an equivalence point.](assets/002-graph-showing-ph-versus-volume-of-naoh-in-cm-ph-.png)

Use the graph to deduce the p*K*<sub>a</sub>1 of the acid.
parts.solution_md:
To deduce the p*K*<sub>a</sub>1 of the acid:

- The equivalence point is 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup>
- At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A<sup>−</sup>], so pH = p*K*<sub>a</sub>1
- Read from the half-equivalence point

  - The volume at which exactly half the NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point has been added

![Graph showing pH change from 2 to 12 as NaOH volume increases from 0 to 35 cm³, with a sharp rise near 25 cm³. Vertical and horizontal lines intersect at 3.15.](assets/003-graph-showing-ph-change-from-2-to-12-as-naoh-vol.png)

p*K*<sub>a</sub>1 = **3.15 ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow any value in the range 3.1 to 3.2

> **[exam-tip]**
> The half-equivalence point is at exactly half the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point. Draw a vertical line from that volume up to the curve, then a horizontal line across to the y-axis — that pH value is p*K*<sub>a</sub>1.
> 
> Make sure you are reading at the half-equivalence point, not the equivalence point itself. The equivalence point is the steepest part of the S-curve; the half-equivalence point is halfway along the x-axis to it.
